lead: These chapters lay the ground for analog and digital communication: the block schematic and the reasons for modulation, signals in time and frequency, the complex envelope of band-pass signals, random variables and random processes, and noise. After them you can compute spectra and complex envelopes, find autocorrelations and power spectral densities, and calculate the noise power, noise figure and noise temperature of a receiver chain.
about: The first chapter draws the communication system as a chain of blocks and gives the reasons for modulation. The next two describe signals in frequency: the Fourier transform with its pairs and properties, then the Hilbert transform, which turns a band-pass signal into its low-pass complex envelope. The middle chapters move to random signals: probability and random variables, then random processes, autocorrelation and power spectral density. The last two apply all of this to noise: where it comes from, why it is modelled as additive white Gaussian noise, and how noise figure and noise temperature measure what a receiver chain adds.

chapters.idea: A communication system moves information from a source to a destination reliably; modulation shifts a baseband message onto a carrier so it can travel through the channel.
chapters.depth: Cover the block schematic: source, transducer, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination; baseband and passband; need for modulation: antenna size, frequency assignment, multiplexing, noise and interference; modulation as frequency translation. Name analog and digital modulation only; some syllabi call the block schematic the communication model. Define carrier, bandwidth and message signal.
chapters.figure: blocks, left to right: Source → Transmitter → Channel → Receiver → Destination; a noise arrow enters the channel block.
chapters.example: A 1 kHz audio tone is to be radiated. Compare quarter-wave antenna lengths at 1 kHz and at a 100 MHz carrier. Use c = 3×10^8 m/s. At 1 kHz, λ = 300 km and λ/4 = 75 km. At 100 MHz, λ = 3 m and λ/4 = 0.75 m. Modulation reduces the antenna from 75 km to 0.75 m.
chapters.trap: Modulation does not create information or reduce noise by itself; it shifts the message spectrum and makes the antenna and multiplexing practical.
chapters.prereq: None; uses basic signals and units from first-year physics.
chapters.leave: AM, FM and PM generation, spectra and demodulation to Units 2 and 3; sampling, quantization and PCM to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Fourier transform maps a signal to its frequency content; a band-pass signal has a narrow spectrum around a carrier and can be handled through its low-pass equivalent.
chapters.depth: Cover Fourier transform and inverse, linearity, time shift, frequency shift, convolution and Parseval/Rayleigh theorem; inverse time-frequency relation; bandwidth definitions; LTI system transmission with h(t) and H(f); distortionless transmission, phase delay and group delay; band-pass signal, centre frequency and bandwidth; canonical form with in-phase and quadrature components. Some syllabi call Parseval theorem Rayleigh energy theorem.
chapters.figure: plot: magnitude spectrum of a low-pass message and a band-pass copy shifted to fc; the band-pass copy is the message spectrum moved around the carrier.
chapters.example: A rectangular pulse x(t) = 2 V for |t| < 0.5 ms and 0 elsewhere. Find X(f), X(0) and the first null-to-null bandwidth. X(f) = A T sinc(fT) = 2×10^-3 sinc(10^3 f) V/Hz; X(0) = 2×10^-3 V/Hz; first null at 1 kHz; null-to-null bandwidth = 2 kHz.
chapters.trap: Bandwidth is not one number; state whether it is first-null, 3-dB or null-to-null. For a rectangular pulse null-to-null is 2/T, not 1/T.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for baseband, carrier and bandwidth terms.
chapters.leave: Hilbert transform and complex envelope to 1.3; random signals and PSD to 1.5.

chapters.idea: Hilbert transform removes negative frequencies to form the analytic signal; the complex envelope is that analytic signal shifted to baseband and carries the in-phase and quadrature information.
chapters.depth: Cover Hilbert transform definition and properties, −90° phase shift; analytic signal or pre-envelope; complex envelope; I and Q components; relation between band-pass and low-pass; downconversion and upconversion; low-pass representation of band-pass systems; phase shifting. Some syllabi call the complex envelope the low-pass equivalent.
chapters.figure: blocks: x(t) → Hilbert transformer → x̂(t); combine to analytic signal xa(t); multiply by e^(−j2πfc t) → complex envelope; real part after upconversion gives x(t).
chapters.example: x(t) = 2 cos(2πfc t + 30°) V. Find the Hilbert transform, analytic signal, complex envelope, and I and Q at t = 0. x̂(t) = 2 sin(2πfc t + 30°); xa(t) = 2e^(j(2πfc t + 30°)); x̃(t) = 2e^(j30°) = 1.732 + j1.000 V; I = 1.732 V, Q = 1.000 V.
chapters.trap: Hilbert transform of cos is sin, not −sin; complex envelope removes the carrier but keeps phase. Do not call x̃(t) the analytic signal.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for Fourier shift and band-pass spectra.
chapters.leave: Modulator and demodulator circuits to Units 2 and 3; SDR implementations to later units.

chapters.idea: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome; its CDF and PDF let us compute the probability that a measured value lies in a range.
chapters.depth: Cover probability axioms, conditional probability and Bayes; random variable, CDF, PDF and PMF; mean, variance and moments; uniform, Gaussian, binomial, Poisson and exponential distributions; joint, marginal, conditional and independence; function of a random variable; central limit theorem statement; characteristic function mention. Some syllabi call this function of random variables.
chapters.figure: plot: Gaussian PDF with mean 0 and σ = 1 and uniform PDF on [−1, 1]; probability is area under the curve.
chapters.example: Gaussian noise voltage has mean 0 and standard deviation 2 mV. Find P(V > 4 mV). z = (4 − 0)/2 = 2; P = Q(2) = 0.0228, about 2.3%.
chapters.trap: PDF height can exceed 1; only area is probability. For nonzero mean, E[V²] = σ² + μ², not σ².
chapters.prereq: 1.2 for integrals and Fourier transform if characteristic functions appear; basic probability from first year.
chapters.leave: Random processes and PSD to 1.5; noise distributions to 1.6.

chapters.idea: A random process is a set of random signals over time; for a WSS process the autocorrelation and its Fourier transform, the PSD, describe average power in time and frequency.
chapters.depth: Cover random process ensemble; mean, variance, autocorrelation and autocovariance; strict-sense and wide-sense stationary; ergodicity; cross-correlation; PSD; Wiener–Khinchine theorem; PSD properties; filtering of random processes with output PSD |H(f)|² Sx(f); average power Rx(0). Some syllabi call PSD the power density spectrum.
chapters.figure: plot: autocorrelation Rx(τ) and its Fourier transform PSD Sx(f) as a transform pair; the area under PSD is average power.
chapters.example: White noise with two-sided PSD N0/2 = 10^-6 W/Hz passes through an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth B = 10 kHz. Find output power. N0 = 2×10^-6 W/Hz; P = N0 B = 2×10^-6 × 10^4 = 0.02 W.
chapters.trap: Rx(0) is average power, not variance unless mean is zero. Two-sided PSD integrates over −∞ to ∞; one-sided over 0 to ∞.
chapters.prereq: 1.4 for expectation and distributions; 1.2 for Fourier transform.
chapters.leave: White noise and AWGN details to 1.6; noise figure to 1.7; receiver filtering to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Noise is unwanted random voltage or current; white noise has a flat PSD and AWGN adds Gaussian noise with a flat spectrum to the signal.
chapters.depth: Cover thermal noise, shot noise, flicker 1/f noise and burst noise; Johnson–Nyquist formula; white noise definition and PSD N0/2; autocorrelation; Gaussian noise and AWGN; noise power in bandwidth; equivalent noise bandwidth; SNR definition; additive noise channel. Some syllabi call thermal noise Johnson noise.
chapters.figure: blocks: signal source → sum junction where AWGN is added → receiver; the noise source has flat PSD.
chapters.example: A 1 kΩ resistor at T = 290 K feeds a receiver of bandwidth 1 MHz. Find available thermal noise power and RMS noise voltage. k = 1.38×10^-23 J/K. P = kTB = 1.38×10^-23 × 290 × 10^6 = 4.00×10^-15 W (−114 dBm). vn = √(4kTRB) = 4.0 μV.
chapters.trap: White noise has infinite total power; always specify bandwidth. N0 and N0/2 differ by 3 dB; match two-sided and one-sided use.
chapters.prereq: 1.5 for PSD and autocorrelation; 1.4 for Gaussian distribution.
chapters.leave: Noise figure and temperature to 1.7; AM and FM noise performance to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Noise figure and noise temperature measure how much a device or receiver degrades SNR; Friis formula gives the overall figure for cascaded stages.
chapters.depth: Cover noise figure F and NF in dB; definition with source at T0 = 290 K; noise temperature Te; F = 1 + Te/T0 and Te = (F − 1)T0; lossy component; cascaded noise figure Friis formula; first stage dominates; input and output SNR. Some syllabi call linear F the noise factor.
chapters.figure: blocks: antenna → stage 1 (G1, F1) → stage 2 (G2, F2) → output; Friis adds the second stage divided by G1.
chapters.example: Two-stage receiver: G1 = 20 dB, F1 = 3 dB; G2 = 20 dB, F2 = 6 dB. Find overall F and Te. Convert: G1 = 100, F1 = 2; G2 = 100, F2 = 4. F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 = 2 + 3/100 = 2.03 (3.07 dB). Te = (2.03 − 1) × 290 = 298.7 K.
chapters.trap: Do not add dB noise figures directly; convert to linear, apply Friis, then convert back. The reference temperature is 290 K, not 300 K.
chapters.leave: Receiver sensitivity and link budgets to later units; AM and FM figure of merit to Unit 3.
